# Reflection {#reflection}

People rarely send the first draft of anything important. They reread it,
notice that "next week" is ambiguous or that a figure is wrong, and fix it.
**Reflection** gives an LLM workflow the same step. The model, or a second
model, reviews an output and produces an improved version.

Reflection is the easiest agentic pattern to add to an existing system. It is
also the easiest one to overrate. This chapter explains how it works, when it
helps, why it often fails without outside information, and how to measure
whether it is worth its cost.

## The basic pattern

A reflection workflow has two or more LLM calls in sequence:

1. **Generate.** Prompt the model for a first draft (version 1).
2. **Critique.** Pass version 1 to a model with a different prompt. Ask it to
   review the draft against stated criteria and list the problems.
3. **Revise.** Ask the model to write version 2 that fixes those problems.

Steps 2 and 3 are often combined into a single "review and rewrite" prompt.
Keeping them separate makes the critique visible, which helps with debugging
and evaluation.

The critique step does not always lead to a rewrite. It can also **filter**:
generate twenty candidate taglines, then have the critic keep only the three
that meet every criterion. Brainstorm-then-filter is often cheaper and safer
than asking for one perfect answer.

**Example.** An analyst asks a model to draft a short client email summarizing
a campaign's results. The first draft says "performance improved last month"
and quotes a click-through rate that does not match the report. A reflection
prompt that says "check every number against the attached report and replace
vague time references with dates" catches both problems. The revised draft
names the month and uses the correct figure.

The same structure works for many outputs:

| Output | What the critique step looks for |
|:-------|:---------------------------------|
| Email or report | Tone, accuracy of facts and promises, missing details, length |
| Code | Bugs, unhandled edge cases, readability |
| Structured data (deeply nested JSON, HTML tables) | Malformed structure, missing fields, wrong types |
| Step-by-step instructions | Missing or out-of-order steps, ambiguity |
| Names, taglines, or brand copy | Hard to pronounce, unintended meanings in the target markets' languages |
| SQL query | Wrong joins, wrong filters, missing date ranges |

### Same model or a different one?

The critic can be the same model with a different prompt, or a different
model. Different models have different strengths. A common configuration
drafts with a fast, cheap model and critiques with a **reasoning model**,
because models that think before answering tend to be better at spotting bugs
and logical gaps. Treat the choice of generator and critic as a configuration
to test, not a fixed rule.

**Background.** Critique-and-revise also appears at training time.
Constitutional AI [@bai2022constitutional] has a model critique and revise its
own responses against written principles, then trains on the revisions
(Section \@ref(scaling-feedback-constitutional-ai-and-rlaif)). Reflection as
discussed here happens at **inference time** and changes no weights.

> **In short.**
>
> - Reflection is generate, critique, revise. The critique can also filter a
>   set of candidates instead of rewriting one.
> - The critic can be the same model or a different one; test which works.
> - It happens at inference time; Constitutional AI uses the same idea at
>   training time.

## What the evidence says

Reflection is not magic. Its effect ranges from large to zero to negative,
depending on the task and on whether the critic has new information.

**Where self-feedback helps.** Self-Refine [@madaan2023selfrefine] used one
model to generate, give feedback on, and refine its own output, with no extra
training and no external tools. Across seven tasks (including dialogue
responses, code optimization, code readability, and constrained generation),
humans and automatic metrics preferred the refined outputs. Task performance
rose by about 20 percentage points on average.

**Where it does not.** In the same paper, math reasoning barely moved: GPT-4
went from 92.9% to 93.1% on GSM8K, and GPT-3.5 did not improve at all. The
authors traced this to the critic. A reasoning chain that *looks* consistent
convinces the model that everything is fine. ChatGPT's feedback was
essentially "everything looks good" for 94% of the math problems. When an
external signal told the model that its answer was wrong, the gains exceeded
5 points.

@huang2024selfcorrect tested **intrinsic self-correction**, where the model
reviews its own answer with no external feedback, on reasoning benchmarks.
Performance did not improve and sometimes fell. For GPT-3.5 on GSM8K,
accuracy went from 75.9% to 75.1% after one round of self-correction and to
74.7% after two, because the model changed some correct answers to wrong ones.
They also showed that some earlier reports of self-correction gains had used
ground-truth labels to decide when to stop, which a deployed system does not
have.

**Where external feedback makes the difference.** Reflexion
[@shinn2023reflexion] has an agent reflect in words on task feedback, such as
the results of unit tests, and store the reflections in memory for its next
attempt. It reached 91% pass@1 on HumanEval, against 80% for GPT-4 used
directly. CRITIC [@gou2024critic] has the model check its output with tools
(search for facts, a code interpreter for programs) before revising. It
improved question answering, mathematical program synthesis, and toxicity
reduction, and its authors stress that the external feedback is what matters.

**Why the pattern looks like this.** A critic that sees only the draft has
the same knowledge and blind spots as the model that wrote it. It catches
problems that are easier to *recognize* than to *avoid*, such as a missing
sign-off, a wrong format, a forgotten requirement, or awkward phrasing. It
tends to miss subtle reasoning errors, and it may "fix" correct answers to
please the reviewer prompt. Models trained on human preferences are prone to
this kind of agreeable over-correction [@sharma2024sycophancy]. New
information breaks the symmetry: the critic now knows something the generator
did not.

The studies side by side:

| Study | Feedback the critic gets | Result |
|:------|:------------------------|:-------|
| Self-Refine [@madaan2023selfrefine] | None (self-feedback) | About +20 points on average across seven tasks; almost nothing on math |
| Huang et al. [@huang2024selfcorrect] | None (intrinsic self-correction) | No gain on reasoning; GPT-3.5 on GSM8K fell slightly |
| Reflexion [@shinn2023reflexion] | Unit-test results, kept in memory | 91% pass@1 on HumanEval vs. 80% for GPT-4 alone |
| CRITIC [@gou2024critic] | Search results, code interpreter | Gains on QA, math programs, and toxicity reduction |

The pattern: the more outside information the critic has, the more reliable
the gain.

> **In short.**
>
> - Self-critique helps on writing, code style, and format, where problems
>   are easy to recognize.
> - It fails on reasoning, and can turn right answers wrong, when the critic
>   has nothing new to go on.
> - External feedback is what makes the gains consistent.

## Reflection with external feedback

External feedback means information from **outside the model** that is added
to the critique step. It is the single most effective way to make reflection
work. Typical sources:

| Source | What it reveals | Example |
|:-------|:----------------|:--------|
| **Code execution** | Errors, stack traces, wrong outputs | Run the generated script; pass the traceback to the critic |
| **Unit tests** | Which behaviors fail | Return failing test names and their assertion messages |
| **Validators** | Schema or format violations | A JSON-schema validator reports missing fields |
| **Rule checks in code** | Policy violations | A regular expression finds competitor names in a draft reply |
| **Counters** | Length limits | Count the words and report "212 words, limit is 150" |
| **Search or retrieval** | Facts the draft got wrong | Retrieve a source and pass the relevant passage to the critic |
| **Database execution** | Empty, huge, or failed results | Run the SQL query and report the row count or error |
| **A human** | Anything a person notices | A reviewer marks a paragraph as off-brand |

Two of these deserve a comment.

- **Length.** LLMs are poor at hitting exact word counts, because they see
  tokens, not words. A few lines of code that count the words and report the
  overshoot fix this more reliably than any amount of prompt tuning.
- **Fact checking.** Suppose a draft states that BLEU and ROUGE were both
  introduced in 2002. A retrieval step finds that BLEU dates from 2002
  [@papineni2002bleu] and ROUGE from 2004 [@lin2004rouge]. Passing those
  passages to the critic turns a plausible error into a specific, fixable
  one.

**Example: the external-feedback loop in code.** The loop below writes a SQL
query, runs it, and feeds any error or suspicious result back to the model.
It stops when the checks pass or after three rounds. The helper names are
illustrative.

```python
def answer_with_sql(question, schema, max_rounds=3):
    query = llm(f"Schema:\n{schema}\n\nWrite one SQL query to answer: {question}")
    for _ in range(max_rounds):
        result = run_sql(query)                 # tool: the outside world
        problems = check(result)                # code, not the model's opinion
        if not problems:
            return query, result                # stop: objective checks pass
        query = llm(
            f"Question: {question}\nQuery:\n{query}\n"
            f"Problems found when running it: {problems}\n"
            "Return a corrected query only."
        )
    return query, None                          # stop: round limit, flag for review

def check(result):
    if result.error:
        return f"Database error: {result.error}"
    if result.row_count == 0:
        return "The query returned no rows. Check filters and date ranges."
    return None
```

Three things make this work. The feedback is specific (the actual error
message). The stop condition is checked by code, not by asking the model if
it is done. And the loop has a hard limit, with a failure path that a human
can pick up.

> **In short.**
>
> - External feedback is information from outside the model: execution
>   results, tests, validators, counters, retrieval, or a human.
> - It is the most effective way to make reflection work.
> - When prompt tuning plateaus, ask what new information the system could
>   get about its own output.

### A practitioner's view of the improvement curve

A pattern many practitioners report, and a useful mental model rather than a
measured law:

- Tuning a single prompt improves quality quickly at first, then plateaus.
- Adding a reflection step and tuning its prompt often lifts the plateau
  somewhat.
- Adding external feedback to the reflection step often lifts it further, and
  keeps improving as the feedback becomes more informative.

So when prompt tuning is showing diminishing returns, ask: **what new
information could the system obtain about its own output?** That question
usually points to the next improvement.

## Multimodal reflection: charts and images

Reflection is not limited to text. A charting workflow can:

1. ask a model to write plotting code for a request such as "compare weekly
   spend and conversions by channel for Q1";
2. run the code to render the chart as an image;
3. give the code, the image, and the original request to a **multimodal
   model** and ask it to critique the chart for readability, clarity, and
   whether it answers the question; and
4. ask for revised code and render again.

The rendered image is a form of external feedback. The critic sees what the
reader will see: overlapping labels, a stacked bar chart that makes
comparisons hard, a missing axis title, or a legend that hides the data. A
first draft might produce stacked bars that bury the comparison. A good
critique recommends grouped bars or a two-panel line chart, and the revision
implements it.

Rendering also catches errors that reading the code would not, such as an
empty plot caused by a wrong column name.

> **In short.**
>
> - A multimodal critic can review a rendered chart, not just the code.
> - The image is external feedback: the critic sees what the reader will see.

## Writing reflection prompts

A reflection prompt is an ordinary prompt (Chapter \@ref(prompt-anatomy)) with
a specific job. What makes it work:

- **Say explicitly that the input is a draft to review**, and what it was
  supposed to achieve. Include the original request.
- **Give concrete criteria.** "Check the tone, verify every date and figure
  against the provided facts, and confirm the call to action is present" works
  better than "improve this".
- **Supply the reference material** the draft should be consistent with: the
  facts, the data, the style guide, the tool outputs.
- **Separate critique from revision** when you want to inspect or evaluate the
  critique, or when a different model should do each part.
- **Allow "no changes needed".** A critic forced to find problems will invent
  them.
- **Ask for structured critique** (a list of issues, each with location and
  fix) when code will act on it, for example to decide whether to run another
  round.

An illustrative critique prompt:

```text
You are reviewing a draft client email written by a junior analyst.

<request>{original_request}</request>
<facts>{campaign_metrics_and_dates}</facts>
<draft>{draft_email}</draft>

Check the draft against these criteria:
1. Every number and date matches <facts>.
2. No promise is made that <facts> does not support.
3. The tone is professional and concise (under 150 words).
4. It ends with a clear next step.

List each problem with the sentence it occurs in and a suggested fix.
If there are no problems, reply exactly: NO_ISSUES.
```

A practical way to learn to write better prompts, reflection prompts
included, is to read prompts from well-regarded open-source agent projects.

> **In short.**
>
> - Say it is a draft, include the original request, and give concrete
>   criteria and reference material.
> - Allow "no changes needed", or the critic will invent problems.
> - Ask for structured critique when code will act on it.

## Design choices and costs

| Choice | Options | Guidance |
|:-------|:--------|:---------|
| Critic model | Same model; a stronger model; a reasoning model | Test combinations on your eval set |
| Rounds | One; a fixed maximum; until a stop condition | One or two rounds capture most of the gain; always cap the loop |
| Stop condition | Critic says no issues; all checks pass; max rounds | Prefer objective checks (tests pass, schema valid) over the critic's opinion |
| Feedback | None; tool results; human | Add external feedback wherever it is cheap to get |
| Scope | Whole output; only the parts that failed a check | Targeted revision reduces drift and cost |

Reflection adds at least one model call per round, so it increases latency
and cost. It can also make things worse: a revision can drift away from
constraints the first draft satisfied, or change a correct answer. Both are
reasons to measure it rather than assume it helps.

> **In short.**
>
> - One or two rounds capture most of the gain; always cap the loop.
> - Stop on objective checks where possible, not on the critic's opinion.
> - Reflection costs latency and money and can make outputs worse, so
>   measure it.

## Measuring whether reflection helps

Before keeping a reflection step, compare the workflow **with** and
**without** it on the same inputs. Chapter \@ref(evaluating-agentic-systems)
develops these ideas fully; here is the version specific to reflection.

**Objective tasks: compare against ground truth.** Suppose a model writes SQL
to answer questions about a retail database, and a reflection step reviews
each query before it runs. Collect a set of questions with known answers,
such as "How many units were sold in May?" or "Which product color has the
highest revenue?". Run both versions and count how often each returns the
correct answer.

Two cautions from basic statistics:

- **Small sets are noisy.** With 15 questions, one question is 6.7
  percentage points. A jump from 13/15 to 14/15 correct is one question and
  could easily be chance. Grow the set as the system matures.
- **Compare paired outcomes.** Both versions answer the same questions, so
  look at the questions where they *disagree*. If reflection fixes five
  answers and breaks one, that is more informative than the two accuracy
  figures alone. McNemar's test formalizes this comparison.

For example, with 40 questions:

|  | Reflection correct | Reflection wrong |
|:--|--:|--:|
| **No reflection correct** | 30 | 1 |
| **No reflection wrong** | 5 | 4 |

Accuracy goes from 31/40 to 35/40. The informative cells are the
disagreements: reflection fixed 5 answers and broke 1. Read those six cases.
They show what the reflection step catches, and what it damages.

The same eval set then lets you compare alternative generation and
reflection prompts quickly, instead of guessing.

**Subjective tasks: use a rubric, not a pairwise vote.** For charts or prose
there is no single right answer, so an **LLM-as-a-judge** is common. The
obvious design, showing the judge both outputs and asking which is better,
has known problems. Judges are sensitive to prompt wording, may disagree with
human experts, and show **position bias**. In @zheng2023judge, Claude-v1
favored whichever answer came first in 75% of swapped pairs under the default
prompt, and GPT-3.5 in 50%. GPT-4 was the most consistent judge but still
favored the first answer in 30% of pairs. The direction is not fixed: with a
reworded prompt, Claude-v1 leaned toward the *second* answer instead. If you
must compare pairs, run each comparison in both orders and count only
consistent verdicts.

A more stable design grades **each output separately against a rubric** of
specific yes/no criteria. For a chart:

- Does it have a clear, descriptive title?
- Are both axes labeled, with units?
- Is the chart type appropriate for the comparison requested?
- Are the axis ranges sensible (no truncated axis exaggerating a change)?
- Can every series be distinguished without relying on color alone?
- Does it answer the question that was asked?

Sum the passes to get a score. In code, the judge returns one 0 or 1 per
criterion as JSON, so the scores can be added up and compared:

```python
RUBRIC = ["clear_title", "axes_labeled_with_units", "appropriate_chart_type",
          "sensible_axis_ranges", "series_distinguishable", "answers_question"]

JUDGE_PROMPT = """Grade this chart against each criterion. Score 1 if it fully
meets the criterion, otherwise 0.
Request: {request}
Criteria: {criteria}
Return JSON only, for example {{"clear_title": 1, "axes_labeled_with_units": 0, ...}}"""

def rubric_score(request, chart_image):
    raw = judge_llm(JUDGE_PROMPT.format(request=request, criteria=RUBRIC),
                    image=chart_image)
    scores = json.loads(raw)
    return sum(scores[c] for c in RUBRIC)          # 0 to 6

with_refl = [rubric_score(r, make_chart(r, reflect=True))  for r in requests]
without   = [rubric_score(r, make_chart(r, reflect=False)) for r in requests]
print(mean(with_refl), mean(without))
```

Each chart is graded on its own, so position bias does not arise. The
per-criterion scores also show *which* criterion reflection improves. Practitioners widely report that several
binary criteria give more consistent judgments than asking for a single 1–5
rating, which models tend to calibrate poorly. Treat this as practitioner
guidance; it is consistent with the evidence on judge instability, but it is
not a settled research result. Check the judge against a sample of human
ratings before trusting it.

**Rule of thumb.** When a criterion is objective, check it with code. Use an
LLM judge only for what code cannot check, and expect to spend time tuning
the rubric.

> **In short.**
>
> - Compare with and without reflection on the same inputs, and read the
>   cases where they disagree.
> - Objective tasks: score against ground truth. Subjective tasks: grade each
>   output against binary rubric items, not pairwise.
> - Small eval sets are noisy; one question out of 15 is almost 7 points.

## Key takeaways

The section summaries above hold the details. The chapter in five lines:

- **What:** generate, critique, revise (or filter), at inference time.
- **When it works:** when problems are easy to recognize, and above all when
  the critic gets external feedback such as test results or retrieved facts.
- **When it fails:** self-critique on reasoning with nothing new to go on.
- **How to build it:** concrete criteria, reference material, "no changes"
  allowed, objective stop conditions, a hard round limit.
- **How to keep it honest:** measure with and without it on the same inputs,
  and judge subjective output with binary rubrics.

## Interview checkpoints

- **What is the reflection pattern?** Generate a draft, critique it against
  criteria, and revise. Same or different model, one or more rounds.
- **Does self-reflection always improve output?** No. Self-Refine reported
  large average gains, but almost none on math reasoning. Huang et al. found
  that intrinsic self-correction did not improve, and sometimes hurt,
  reasoning accuracy.
- **Why does external feedback help so much?** A critic with only the draft
  shares the generator's knowledge and blind spots. Test results, error
  messages, or retrieved facts give it information the generator lacked.
- **Give three cheap sources of external feedback.** Running the code, a
  schema validator, a regular-expression check, a word counter, a database
  query's row count or error, a retrieval-based fact check.
- **Your prompt tuning has plateaued. What do you try next?** Add a reflection
  step, and better still, find external feedback the system can gather about
  its own output.
- **Why might you use a different model for the critique?** Models differ in
  strengths. Reasoning models are often better at finding bugs and logical
  gaps than at fast drafting.
- **How do you decide whether to keep a reflection step?** Run the workflow
  with and without it on the same labeled inputs. Compare accuracy, look at
  which examples changed, and weigh the gain against the extra latency and
  cost.
- **Why is "which of these two outputs is better?" a weak LLM-judge design?**
  Position bias and prompt sensitivity. Grade each output against a rubric of
  binary criteria instead, or at least evaluate both orders.
- **How do you stop a reflection loop?** When objective checks pass, when the
  critic reports no issues, or at a maximum number of rounds, whichever comes
  first.
- **How does Constitutional AI relate to reflection?** It uses the same
  critique-and-revise idea, but at training time to produce training data.
  Reflection in a workflow happens at inference time and changes no weights.
